tagline: Cleaning tasks that get more urgent the longer you leave them.
verdictSummary: Tody's idea is one good mechanic: a task is not due or not due, it decays continuously from clean towards dirty at a rate you set, so the app always answers "what most needs doing right now" instead of showing an overdue list you learn to ignore. Implementing that is arithmetic over a last-done timestamp — a sitting, with no key, no service and nothing to reproduce.
coreLoopDIY: Keep a list of household tasks with an interval each, and see them sorted continuously by how overdue they are, not by whether they crossed a line.
whatYouLose: the mobile apps, which is where you mark a task done, standing in the room
sync between everyone in the house, which is the paid tier
the visual room-by-room layout that makes it feel like a game
the starter task library, so you begin from an empty list
whyPeopleStillPay: Ten dollars a year for something already on the phone in your pocket when you notice the bathroom, and nothing to run.
prompt:
Build a household task tracker around continuous decay rather than due dates.

A task has a name, a room, an interval in days, and a last-done timestamp. Its state is a single number: days since last done, divided by the interval. Below 1.0 it is fine; above, it is overdue by that factor. Everything the tool does is a sort on that number.

The main screen is one list, ordered by that ratio descending, with a colour ramp rather than a binary badge. Nothing is ever "overdue" in a way that accumulates guilt — a task at 3.2 is simply above a task at 1.4, and doing it resets it. That difference in framing is the entire reason this design works where a to-do list does not.

Marking done is one tap and writes a completion row. Never delete history: the completion log is what lets the tool suggest a better interval, by comparing how often you actually do a task with the interval you claimed.

Add a "I have twenty minutes" view: given a duration you enter, pick the highest-ratio tasks whose estimated durations fit, and show them as a short list. That single feature is what turns a tracker into something used on a Saturday morning.

Add room filtering and a per-room summary, since cleaning happens by room rather than by priority.

Run it as an offline-first progressive web app with local storage, syncing when it can reach your server. If more than one person uses it, merge by last-write-wins on the completion timestamp — completions are idempotent enough that this is genuinely fine.

Do not add streaks or a score. A cleaning app that makes you feel bad about a bad week gets deleted during the bad week.

faq.q: Can I import my Tody tasks?
faq.a: No — Tody has no export, so the task list is retyped. It is twenty minutes for a normal house, and writing the list yourself is arguably the useful part.

faq.q: How do I pick the intervals?
faq.a: Guess, then let the completion log correct you. After two months, compare each task's median actual gap against its configured interval and adjust — the guessed number matters much less than having the history to fix it with.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing locally. A few dollars a month if you host it so several phones can share one list, which is more than the subscription.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Marking it done in the moment. Tody is on the phone in your hand when you notice the skirting boards, and a web app you have to remember to open catches the tasks you think about rather than the ones you see.
